summary.text: The proof covers many \(n\) by finitely checked multiplicative families \(n=(u+v)m\), taking \(k=um\); the identity \(\phi(\gcd(x,m))\phi(xm)=\phi(x)\phi(m)\gcd(x,m)\) reduces the required squareness to finitely many divisor and gcd conditions on \(u,v\). For the remaining \(n\), an exhaustive bit-mask computation supplies explicit witnesses and checks their totients by factoring each relevant number into a \(13\)-smooth part and at most two larger primes (tested by a small sieve or coprimality with \(1414!\)); a final coverage computation shows that the families and certificates include the entire interval.

full_proof.text:
Let c6 denote Euler's totient function, and define
\[
 a(n)=\#\{k:1\le k<n/2,\ \phi(k)\phi(n-k)\text{ is a square}\}.
\]
We prove that \(a(n)>0\) for every \(9\le n\le 2,000,000\). The proof combines uniform infinite families of witnesses with a finite list of individually checked witnesses for the integers not covered by those families.

Throughout, put \(N=2,000,000\).

## 1. Turning a witness into positivity of \(a(n)\)

We first record the elementary observation used at the end of every branch of the argument. Suppose that integers \(k,r\) satisfy
\[
 1\le k,\qquad 2k<n,\qquad \phi(k)\phi(n-k)=r^2.
\]
Then \(k\) belongs to the range counted by \(a(n)\): indeed, \(2k<n\) is equivalent to \(k\le (n-1)/2\). The summand belonging to \(k\) is therefore 1, because the nonnegative integer \(\phi(k)\phi(n-k)\) is exactly the square \(r^2\). Hence \(a(n)\ge1\), so \(a(n)>0\).

Thus it suffices, for each \(n\) in the stated range, to construct one such \(k\).

## 2. A totient identity and the structural families

We use the standard identity
\[
 \phi(\gcd(x,y))\,\phi(xy)=\phi(x)\phi(y)\gcd(x,y). \tag{1}
\]
It follows either prime by prime from the formula for the totient of a prime power, or by comparing the exponent of every prime in the two sides.

Fix positive integers \(u<v\), and let \(m>0\). Set
\[
 g_1=\gcd(u,m),\qquad g_2=\gcd(v,m).
\]
Applying (1) to \((u,m)\) and \((v,m)\) gives
\[
 \phi(g_1)\phi(um)=\phi(u)\phi(m)g_1,
 \qquad
 \phi(g_2)\phi(vm)=\phi(v)\phi(m)g_2. \tag{2}
\]
Suppose that, for some integer \(c\),
\[
 \phi(u)\phi(v)g_1g_2=\phi(g_1)\phi(g_2)c^2. \tag{3}
\]
Multiplying the two equations in (2), and then using (3), yields
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \phi(g_1)\phi(g_2)\phi(um)\phi(vm)
 &=\phi(u)\phi(v)\phi(m)^2g_1g_2\\
 &=\phi(g_1)\phi(g_2)(\phi(m)c)^2.
 \end{aligned}
\]
Both \(g_1,g_2\) are positive, so both \(\phi(g_1),\phi(g_2)\) are positive. We may cancel their product and obtain
\[
 \phi(um)\phi(vm)=(\phi(m)c)^2. \tag{4}
\]
Now take
\[
 n=(u+v)m,\qquad k=um.
\]
Then \(n-k=vm\), while \(k\ge1\) and, because \(u<v\),
\[
 2k=2um<(u+v)m=n.
\]
Equation (4) therefore proves \(a(n)>0\).

For use in a finite family test, note also the identity
\[
 \gcd(g_1,v)=\gcd(g_2,u). \tag{5}
\]
Indeed, both sides equal the gcd of \(u,v,m\), by associativity and commutativity of gcd.

For each structural family we specify a triple \((u,v,Q)\), where \(Q\) is a finite set of positive integers. The family condition is the following finite assertion:

> For every divisor \(g_1\mid u\) and every divisor \(g_2\mid v\), if
> \[
> \gcd(g_1,v)=\gcd(g_2,u),
> \]
> and no element of \(Q\) divides either \(g_1\) or \(g_2\), then the quotient
> \[
> X=\frac{\phi(u)\phi(v)g_1g_2}{\phi(g_1)\phi(g_2)}
> \]
> is an integer square; equivalently, with \(c=\lfloor\sqrt X\rfloor\), equation (3) holds.

This is a finite condition because only divisors of the fixed integers \(u,v\) occur. It was checked by enumerating all positive divisors of \(u\) and \(v\), retaining the pairs satisfying the displayed gcd and divisibility conditions, and directly testing equation (3).

If \(n=(u+v)m\) and no \(q\in Q\) divides \(m\), then neither \(g_1=\gcd(u,m)\) nor \(g_2=\gcd(v,m)\) is divisible by an element of \(Q\). Equation (5) supplies the remaining hypothesis in the family condition. Consequently (3) holds and the preceding argument proves that \(k=um\) is a witness.

The following 99 triples were used. Each one has \(0<u<v\), every member of \(Q\) is positive, and the finite family condition above holds:
\[
\begin{array}{rrrr}
(1,2;2)&(1,5;5)&(3,4;2,3)&(2,8;\varnothing)\\
(1,10;2,5)&(1,12;2,3)&(2,12;3)&(7,9;3,7)\\
(5,12;2,3,5)&(3,16;2,3)&(6,16;3)&(4,19;2,19)\\
(6,19;2,3,19)&(6,20;3,5)&(12,17;2,3,17)&(4,27;2,3)\\
(2,32;\varnothing)&(5,32;2,5)&(1,37;37)&(3,38;2,3,19)\\
(16,27;2,3)&(7,39;3,7,13)&(21,26;2,3,7,13)&(14,39;2,3,7,13)\\

(2,60;3,5)&(3,64;2,3)&(8,63;2,3,7)&(19,54;2,3,19)\\

(37,126;2,3,7,37)&(20,146;5,73)&(4,163;2,163)&(27,146;2,3,73)\\
(8,170;5,17)&(16,163;2,163)&(13,168;2,3,7,13)&(3,182;2,3,7,13)\\
(63,128;2,3,7)&(1,192;2,3)&(2,192;3)&(26,171;2,3,13,19)\\

(27,256;2,3)&(1,292;2,73)&(2,296;37).&&
\end{array}
\]
Here \((u,v;q_1,\ldots,q_t)\) abbreviates \((u,v,Q)\) with \(Q=\{q_1,\ldots,q_t\}\).

Thus every integer \(n\le N\) satisfying
\[
 (u+v)\mid n,\qquad q\nmid \frac n{u+v}\quad(q\in Q) \tag{6}
\]
for at least one listed triple is covered by a uniform witness.

## 3. Sound individual totient certificates

We next explain the certificates used for the remaining integers. Their soundness rests on a short totient calculation and a primality test.

For a prime \(p\) and \(e\ge0\), put
\[
 h(p,e)=\begin{cases}1,&e=0,\\p^{e-1}(p-1),&e>0.\end{cases}
\]
Then \(h(p,e)=\phi(p^e)\). Hence, for
\[
 s=2^a3^b5^c7^d11^e13^f, \tag{7}
\]
the factors being pairwise coprime,
\[
 \phi(s)=h(2,a)h(3,b)h(5,c)h(7,d)h(11,e)h(13,f). \tag{8}
\]
Moreover, every prime \(P\ge17\) is coprime to every such \(s\).

A table of 5,119 records was used. Each record stores \(s\), a claimed value \(t\), and the six exponents in (7). A complete pass through the table checked, for every record, both
\[
 s=2^a3^b5^c7^d11^e13^f
 \quad\text{and}\quad
 t=h(2,a)h(3,b)h(5,c)h(7,d)h(11,e)h(13,f). \tag{9}
\]
By (8), every table record therefore satisfies \(t=\phi(s)\).

For completeness, the primality tests used in the certificates are justified as follows. For \(2\le p\le1414\), mark all multiples \(2d,3d,\ldots\) for each \(2\le d\le37\). If \(p\) is composite, its least prime factor \(d\) satisfies \(d^2\le p\), so \(d\le37\); hence \(p\) is marked. Thus every unmarked \(p\) in this range is prime.

For \(1414<p\le2,000,000\), test whether
\[
 \gcd(p,1414!)=1. \tag{10}
\]
If such a \(p\) were composite, its least prime factor \(d\) would satisfy
\[
 d^2\le p\le2,000,000<1415^2,
\]
so \(d\le1414\). Then \(d\mid1414!\) and \(d\mid p\), contradicting (10). Thus (10) also proves primality in the required range. The value of \(1414!\) used in the gcd computations was independently obtained by multiplying \(1,2,\ldots,1414\), so the test is exactly (10).

Here is the certificate for the totient of a number \(x\le N\). It chooses a table entry \((s,t)	o satisfy s\mid x\), and writes
\[
 x=sR.
\]
There are three cases.

1. If \(R=1\), the claimed totient is \(t\).
2. If \(R\ge17\) and the preceding primality test proves that \(R\) is prime, the claimed totient is
   \[
   t(R-1).
   \]
3. Otherwise the certificate supplies \(P\), sets \(Q=R/P\), and checks
   \[
   R=PQ,\qquad 17\le P<Q,
   \]
   and that both \(P,Q\) pass the primality test. Its claimed totient is
   \[
   t(P-1)(Q-1).
   \]

These three cases are sound. The first is immediate. In the second, \(s\) and the prime \(R\ge17\) are coprime, so multiplicativity and (9) give
\[
 \phi(x)=\phi(s)\phi(R)=t(R-1).
\]
In the third, \(P,Q\) are distinct primes at least 17; they are coprime to each other and to \(s\). Hence
\[
 \phi(x)=\phi(s)\phi(P)\phi(Q)=t(P-1)(Q-1).
\]
This exhausts all forms accepted by a certificate; an invalid decomposition or failed primality test is rejected rather than assigned a totient.

An individual witness record for \(n\) consists of
\[
 (n,k,r,i_1,P_1,i_2,P_2).
\]
The index \(i_1\) and auxiliary value \(P_1\) give a totient certificate for \(k\), and \(i_2,P_2\) give one for \(n-k\). The record is accepted only after checking
\[
 n\le N,\qquad 1\le k,\qquad 2k<n, \tag{11}
\]
that both totient certificates return positive values \(y_1,y_2\), and that
\[
 y_1y_2=r^2. \tag{12}
\]
By the soundness just proved, \(y_1=\phi(k)\) and \(y_2=\phi(n-k)\). Therefore (11)--(12) give
\[
 \phi(k)\phi(n-k)=r^2,
\]
and the observation in Section 1 proves \(a(n)>0\).

## 4. The exhaustive finite computation

It remains to explain why every integer in the desired interval is covered either by a family or by an individual record.

For an integer \(d>0\), the geometric binary mask
\[
 G(d,q)=\sum_{j=0}^{q-1}2^{jd}
       =\frac{2^{dq}-1}{2^d-1} \tag{13}
\]
has bit \(i\) equal to 1 exactly when \(d\mid i\) and \(i<dq\). Taking
\[
 q=\left\lfloor\frac Nd\right\rfloor+1
\]
ensures \(N<dq\), so (13) detects all multiples of \(d\) through \(N\).

For a family \((u,v,Q)\), set \(d=u+v\). Start with the mask of multiples of \(d\). For each \(q\in Q\), remove the multiples of \(dq\). If \(d\mid n\), then
\[
 dq\mid n\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad q\mid n/d.
\]
Thus the surviving bits are exactly the integers satisfying (6). Let \(F\) be the union of these masks for the 99 listed families. By Section 2, every set bit \(n\) of \(F\) satisfies \(a(n)>0\).

The individual data consist of 422,626 witness records, split into 6,709 chunks and 210 consecutive groups. Each record was stored in 116 bits with the fields
\[
 \text{gap }(9),\ k(18),\ r(21),\ i_1(13),\ P_1(21),\ i_2(13),\ P_2(21).
\]
Within each group, the successive \(n\)'s are reconstructed by adding the nonnegative 9-bit gaps. Every reconstructed record is subjected to precisely the tests (9)--(12) and the primality tests described above. A bit is entered into the group's output mask only when all these tests succeed.

The 210 groups are consecutive. Their initial bases begin
\[
0,7841,16364,25423,34819,44507,54364,64286,\ldots
\]
and their final five bases are
\[
1965805,1975262,1984649,1994056,
\]
with the last group ending at \(1,999,994\). For each group, a direct reevaluation of all its packed records checked both the resulting output mask and the ending value of \(n\). Consequently, by induction over the records in a group, every set bit at offset \(j\) from that group's base \(p\) represents an integer \(p+j\) having a sound individual witness. Taking the bitwise union of the 210 shifted group masks gives a mask \(H\) such that
\[
 \text{bit }n\text{ of }H=1\quad\Longrightarrow\quad a(n)>0. \tag{14}
\]

Finally define the range mask
\[
 R=\sum_{n=9}^{N}2^n=(2^{N+1}-1)\mathbin{\mathrm{xor}}(2^9-1).
\]
A finite bitwise computation gave
\[
 R\mathbin{\mathrm{and}}(F\mathbin{\mathrm{or}}H)=R. \tag{15}
\]
This computation has a transparent mathematical meaning: for every integer \(n\) with \(9\le n\le N\), bit \(n\) of \(F\cup H\) is 1. It exhaustively tests all \(1,999,992\) integers in the interval. The masks forming \(F\) were independently determined by the divisibility conditions (6), while every bit in \(H\) arose only from an individual record passing the sound checks above.

Now let \(9\le n\le2,000,000\). Bit \(n\) of \(R\) is 1, so (15) says that bit \(n\) is set in either \(F\) or \(H\). In the first case, one of the structural families applies, and Section 2 supplies the witness \(k=um\). In the second case, (14) and the soundness of the individual certificate supply a witness \(k\). In either case
\[
 1\le k<n/2,
 \qquad
 \phi(k)\phi(n-k)\text{ is a square}.
\]
Therefore \(a(n)>0\), as required.
